characterList.description: An orange, Pacman-shaped structure embedded in the cell membrane. It has three binding sites for sodium ions on one side and two binding sites for potassium ions on the other side.
characterList.name: Sodium-Potassium Pump

characterList.description: A purple, Pacman-shaped structure embedded in the cell membrane. It has two binding sites for sodium ions and one for a glucose molecule.
characterList.name: Sodium-Glucose Transporter

characterList.description: A light blue oval structure embedded in the cell membrane. It is always open, allowing potassium ions to pass through.
characterList.name: Potassium Leak Channel

characterList.description: Represented by a larger yellow star that binds to the Sodium-Potassium Pump.
characterList.name: ATP

activities.description: Sodium and potassium ions are shown distributed unevenly across a cell membrane, with more sodium outside and more potassium inside.
The Sodium-Potassium Pump appears embedded in the cell membrane.

characterInteraction.description: The introduction showing their roles in maintaining cell membrane potential.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Introduces fundamental concepts necessary for understanding subsequent scenes.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Introduction of ion concentrations and the Sodium-Potassium Pump sparks curiosity.

narrativeProgression.description: Establishes the context of the video by illustrating the uneven distribution of sodium and potassium ions and introducing the Sodium-Potassium Pump.

scenes.thematicElements: The importance of maintaining ion gradients in living cells.
scenes.title: Introduction of Ion Concentrations and the Sodium-Potassium Pump

activities.description: The Sodium-Potassium Pump binds three sodium ions from the intracellular space.
ATP binds to the pump, causing a conformational change that opens the pump towards the extracellular space.
The sodium ions are released into the extracellular space.
The pump binds two potassium ions from the extracellular space, causing the release of the phosphate group from ATP.
Another conformational change occurs, opening the pump towards the intracellular space and releasing the potassium ions.

characterInteraction.description: Sodium ions bind to the Sodium-Potassium Pump and are transported out of the cell.
Potassium ions are transported into the cell by the Sodium-Potassium Pump.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Details the active transport process critical to cellular function.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Explanation of Sodium-Potassium Pump induces a clear understanding.

narrativeProgression.description: Delves deeper into the function of the Sodium-Potassium Pump, demonstrating how it maintains the concentration gradients of sodium and potassium ions across the cell membrane.

scenes.thematicElements: Active transport, energy consumption (ATP hydrolysis), conformational changes in proteins.
scenes.title: Functioning of the Sodium-Potassium Pump

activities.description: The Sodium-Glucose Transporter appears on the membrane and binds two sodium ions and one glucose molecule from the extracellular space.
A conformational change occurs, transporting the sodium and glucose into the intracellular space.
The Potassium Leak Channel is shown allowing potassium ions to move out of the cell, following their concentration gradient.

characterInteraction.description: Sodium and glucose are transported into the cell by the Sodium-Glucose Transporter.
Potassium ions exit the cell through the Potassium Leak Channel.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Illustrates interconnected transport processes essential for cellular nutrient uptake.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Understanding the link between Sodium-Potassium Pump and glucose uptake.

narrativeProgression.description: Expands the scope of the video by showing how the sodium gradient created by the Sodium-Potassium Pump is utilized by other transport mechanisms, like the Sodium-Glucose Transporter.

scenes.thematicElements: Coupled transport, facilitated diffusion, membrane permeability, co-transport.
scenes.title: Coupling of the Sodium-Potassium Pump with the Sodium-Glucose Transporter

activities.description: Potassium ions continue to flow out of the cell through the Potassium Leak Channel.
Plus and minus signs appear on either side of the membrane, indicating the electrical charges resulting from the ion movements.

characterInteraction.description: Sodium and potassium ions play a role in establishing the resting membrane potential through their respective channels and pumps.
These components interact to stabilize the resting membrane potential.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Sums up ion transport processes crucial for cellular electrochemical balance.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Final understanding of the resting membrane potential formation.

narrativeProgression.description: Concludes the explanation by showing how the net movement of positive ions out of the cell creates a negative charge inside the cell, resulting in the resting membrane potential.

scenes.thematicElements: Resting membrane potential, electrical charge, membrane potential, electrochemical gradient.
scenes.title: Establishing the Resting Membrane Potential

climax.description: The resting membrane potential is established.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: In living cells, the concentration of sodium is much greater outside the cell than it
is inside the cell, and potassium is much greater inside the cell than outside.
The sodium potassium pump is a main mechanism used by cells in order to maintain the concentration
gradient of these two ions.
It functions by binding three sodium ions.
Followed by ATP indicated by the star, ATP hydrolysis phosphorylates the pump and induces
a conformational change.
The phosphorylated form has decreased affinity for sodium, allowing the sodium to diffuse
away.
The pump binds two potassium ions outside of the cell, which causes release of the phosphate
and induces a conformational change, which then releases potassium and allows the cycle
to start again.
The sodium which leaves the cell is used to bring larger molecules, such as glucose,
back into the cell, by moving down its concentration gradient using a carrier.
The purple sodium glucose transporter functions by binding two sodium ions and one glucose
molecule.
A conformational change causes the sodium and glucose to enter the cell.
Other mechanisms such as this, large molecules, such as glucose, would not be able to enter
the cell.
The potassium, which enters the cell, leaves through the light blue potassium-leach channel,
which is always open.
This makes the cell more permeable to potassium than any other ion.
The potassium-leach channel, combined with the sodium potassium pump, which removes more
positive ions than it brings in, causes the cell to have a negative resting potential,
and allows the cell to manipulate the environment to suit its needs.
